Qian Wu®, Yufei Chen, Wei Liu®, Xiaodong Yue®, and Xiahai Zhuang
Abstract—Accurately segmenting tubular structures,
such as blood vessels or nerves, holds significant clinical
implications across various medical applications. However,
existing methods often exhibit limitations in achieving
satisfactory topological performance, particularly in terms
of preserving connectivity. To address this challenge,
we propose a novel deep-learning approach, termed Deep
Closing, inspired by the well-established classic closing
operation. Deep Closing first leverages an AutoEncoder
trained in the Masked Image Modeling (MIM) paradigm,
enhanced with digital topology knowledge, to effectively
learn the inherent shape prior of tubular structures and
indicate potential disconnected regions. Subsequently,
a Simple Components Erosion module is employed to
generate topology-focused outcomes, which refines the
preceding segmentation results, ensuring all the generated
regions are topologically significant. To evaluate the
efficacy of Deep Closing, we conduct comprehensive
experiments on 4 datasets: DRIVE, CHASE_DB1, DCA1, and
CREMI. The results demonstrate that our approach yields
considerable improvements in topological performance
compared with existing methods. Furthermore, Deep Clos-
ing exhibits the ability to generalize and transfer knowledge
from external datasets, showcasing its robustness and
adaptability. The code for this paper has been available at:
https://github.com/5k5000/DeepClosing.

I. INTRODUCTION
UBULAR structures constitute significant anatomical
.features present in various medical images, encompassing
entities such as blood vessels and airways. Despite the
remarkable achievements of deep learning methodologies in
medical image segmentation [1], [2], the segmentation of
tubular structures remains a formidable endeavor, largely due
to their intricate morphologies and diverse scales [3], [4].
Fig. 1.
An illustration of the Classic Closing Operation and the
proposed Deep Closing. The traditional closing operation compromises
two steps: Dilation and Erosion, which first generate new foreground
points alongside borders and then eliminate part of them with
predetermined kernels. Correspondingly, our approach introduces two
enhanced constituents: Deep Dilation, which involves the indication of
disconnection regions through the reconstruction process of a masked
AutoEncoder (MAE) embedded with tubular shape prior; and Simple
Component Erosion to filter out topologically insignificant regions.
It often encounters challenges in preserving continuity within
diminutive and low signal-to-noise regions, thereby risking
the disruption of structural topology. This issue predominantly
emerges from the substantial intra-class variance apparent in
pixel-level features within these localized regions.
The issue of connectivity defects in medical tubular
structures is somewhat different from those in general
segmentation tasks where the models typically aim to achieve
better overlapping-based performance, i.e. higher Dice score.
The disconnected regions tend to appear in thin and tiny
parts which may have minimal effects on the overall
overlapping-oriented optimization, thus usually causing the
problem of disconnection under-focused. To surmount this
challenge, some researchers have designed topology-aware
methods [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11] which typically
impose extra topological constraints or networks designs
during optimization. Some propose to enhance topological
performance based on label refinement [12], [13], [14] which
typically cascades multiple networks and makes the following
ones serve as label error fixers for preceding ones. Besides,
some general post-processing methods for segmentation like
ConvCRF [15], CascadePSP [16] and Segrefiner [17], also
show some effectiveness in mitigating the disconnection issue.
The limitations of topology-aware methods, label refinement
techniques, and post-processing strategies in medical image
segmentation, particularly for tubular structures, present
unique challenges. Topology-aware methods, despite incorpo-
rating topological constraints, are predominantly guided by the
overlapping-based segmentation loss in an end-to-end training
pattern. This dominance of segmentation loss means that any
improvements in topological performance could be inherently
limited, as the primary optimization direction remains focused
on segmentation accuracy. Label refinement methods carry the
risk of overfitting specific refinement criteria, limiting their
generalizability to other models and making them primarily
applicable only to the original models that they were trained
with. Post-processing methods, while effective in the context
of natural images, tend to underperform when applied to
medical tubular datasets. This ineffectiveness is often due to
the specialized nature of medical images, where the structural
complexity and the critical importance of accurate topology
present challenges that standard post-processing techniques
cannot handle.
To address the above challenges, we aim to design a
shape-oriented connectivity-enhancing method that is model-
agnostic, generalizable, and can perform even when source
images are unavailable. Following this purpose, we turn
our attention to the classic closing operation, a technique
specifically designed to bridge minor gaps within shapes.
The Closing operation constitutes a foundational technique
within image processing, assuming particular significance
within the field of both medical image and natural image
analysis. However, on the one hand, the judicious choice of the
structuring elements like kernel size in the closing operation
assumes paramount importance, as an improperly chosen
size may result in insufficient gap closure or unintended
amalgamation and smoothing of neighboring structures. On the
other hand, though easy to implement and generalizable,
the performance of this conventional technique is essentially
limited.
Motivated by this, we propose a novel deep learning
approach that extends the traditional closing operation,
as shown in Fig.1. We replace the dilation process with the
reconstruction of a designed Masked AutoEncoder, called
Deep Dilation, and the erosion process with the proposed
Simple Component Erosion operation. This approach leverages
pre-trained knowledge to learn the intrinsic shape prior of
tubular structures and focuses on the connectivity information
to identify and refine the segmentation results.
Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) As
generally shown in Fig. 1, we propose a novel paradigm
that revisits the classic closing operation with deep learning
techniques to enhance connectivity in the segmentation of
medical tubular structures. (2) We design a Simple Point
Erosion module based on Digital Topology knowledge, which
could efficiently deplete points that will not affect the
topology under a paralleled pipeline, hereby identifying the
topologically critical ones. This module could be integrated
into the proposed framework and provide enhanced topological
guidance. (3) Our extensive experiments demonstrate the
effectiveness of improving topological performance and the
transferability of our approach to learn from external datasets,
enhancing overall segmentation performance.
II. RELATED WORKS
A. Topology-Aware Segmentation
Deep Learning methods have achieved huge success in
medical segmentation [1], [18], [19], [20], [21], and most of
them are optimized towards better overlap between prediction
and target. However, in such a setting, topological coherence
is often attached with less significance during optimization as
it contributes little to the overall performance when measured
with overlap-based metrics, such as Dice and IOU [9].
To improve the topological performance in tubular struc-
tures, some researchers propose adding topological constraints
during optimization in order to guide models to focus on
preserving topology. The core idea of these methods is to
identify a group of topologically critical points and then
impose an extra penalty on them. Hu et al. [5] first propose
to utilize the persistence diagram to enforce the topology
consistency between the prediction and ground truth. After
that, they propose Discrete Morse Theory (DMT) Loss [6]
which uses the Morse complex of the likelihood map
to generate skeletons as topological constraints with time
complexity of O(nlog(n)). They later simplify the critical
points searching process with an efficient homotopy warping
operation [7], theoretically achieving a time complexity of
O(n). However, it's worth noting that while this technique
offers advantages, it may not always guarantee the identifica-
tion of all topologically critical points and involves operations
that can be computationally intensive on CPUs, such as depth
distance transform and pixel-wise loops. The authors of [9]
propose a novel, efficient, and differentiable skeletonization
approach, called Centerline Dice (Cldice). They further
introduce an additional loss on the computed centerlines of
prediction and labels, in order to emphasize connectivity.
However, their proposed skeletonization approach represents
an approximation and may result in disconnected segments on
centerlines. Stucki et al. [22] point out that the Wasserstein
matching adopted in [5] could not always guarantee spatially
correct matching and introduce a Betti Matching method to
address such issue.
Beyond designing pixel-level topological constrains,
Hu et al. [8] also pioneer another branch of methods in
learning probabilistic topological representation, which
could perform structure-level sampling, together with
uncertainty, thus leading to better topological integrity.
Gupta et al. [23] design a more fine-grained probabilistic
structural representation learning by introducing a probabilistic
DMT model, and further consider both inter-structure
and intra-structure uncertainty, yielding more promising
uncertainty maps.
PointScatter [10] designs a point prediction and regression
paradigm for tubular structure segmentation, which could
be utilized as an auxiliary task and embedded into existing
methods, in order to enhance topological performance.

B. Enhancing Topological Performance via Label
Refinement and Post-Processing
To enhance the topological performance, another approach
is to conduct a secondary analysis of the pre-computed results
using post-processing methods [24], [25], [26], [27]. These
methods introduce additional topological constraints to the
likelihood maps. In recent years, researchers have also adopted
deep learning-based approaches to develop multi-stage or
cascaded methods for improving topological performance.
One such method, DoubleUnet [13], combines two UNet
[1] structures and implicitly embeds the target of topology
enhancement into the overall optimization process. Another
approach, DVAE-refiner [12], proposes cascading a denoising
variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) after a typical segmentation
network. The VAE module first encodes precomputed shapes
into a compact latent space and then reconstructs new ones
to yield refined results. ErrorNet [14] cascades a noise-
injected VAE to synthesize label errors and then trains another
convolutional network to learn the synthetic error residue.
During the inference stage, ErrorNet fuses segmentation
results and error-corrected regions to yield better overall
outcomes.
Beyond the aforementioned model-specific label refinement
techniques, whose effectiveness is often contingent upon
preceding models, several general post-processing strategies
can also contribute to the enhancement of segmentation
quality in tubular structures. These include morphological
closing operations, Conditional Random Fields (CRF) [28],
CascadePSP [16], and SegRefiner [17]. Notably, these
approaches are not limited by model or class specificity,
suggesting their broad applicability and potential in improving
segmentation outcomes.
C. Masked Image Modeling & Denoising AutoEncoder
Recently, the autoregressive paradigm of masking and
reconstruction has garnered significant attention from
researchers in the field of computer vision. Notable
contributions in this area include BEiT [29], MAE [30],
and Simmim [31]. While these works primarily focus on
pretraining Transformer architectures [32], [33], we have
discovered that the technique of masking images can be
adapted and modified to efficiently generate synthetic
disconnected errors for tubular structures. Denoising
AutoEncoders are neural networks that are trained to
reconstruct clean data from noisy or corrupted inputs.
By introducing a masking mechanism, where certain
regions of the input are intentionally masked or corrupted,
denoising AutoEncoders can learn to effectively recover
the missing or corrupted information. This approach
has shown promising results in various applications,
including image denoising, inpainting, and now, in the
generation of synthetic disconnected errors for tubular
structures.

the trained AutoEncoder in previous steps with the Simple
Component Erosion (a derivative operation of the Simple Point

V. CONCLUSION
We propose a post-processing method that effectively
identifies potential disconnected regions in tubular structures.
While end-to-end approaches are currently favored, we believe
our method holds significant value for the following reasons:
(1) Our method has the potential to further improve the
topological performance of existing end-to-end methods. (2)
In situations where privacy concerns or limited data acces-
sibility prevent access to the original data, our method can
produce enhanced outcomes via analyzing shape information
alone. (3) Unlike end-to-end approaches, our method generates
new topologically critical regions without altering the original
output. This makes it more explainable and suitable for
interactive diagnosis. (4) Even when both image and label data
are inaccessible, our method can transfer the learned inherent
shape prior from other datasets to the target field.
In this paper, we introduce a novel framework that
redefines traditional morphological closing operations through
the integration of advanced deep learning techniques.
Our approach utilizes the reconstruction capabilities of a
trained masked AutoEncoder, which we term Deep Dilation,
to effectively highlight areas of disconnection. Additionally,
we have developed a module called Simple Point Erosion,
aimed at identifying topologically critical points by selectively
eroding non-essential ones (simple points). This further leads
to the design of a novel operation, Simple Component Erosion,
designed to eliminate topologically insignificant components
within structures.
Our proposed framework comprises these two innovative
operations. It demonstrates significant potential in identifying
regions of disconnection, thereby enhancing the topological
performance of medical tubular segmentation. Moreover,
our method exhibits a strong capability to transfer shape
priors from external datasets, showcasing its versatility and
effectiveness across different applications.

V. CONCLUSION
We propose a post-processing method that effectively
identifies potential disconnected regions in tubular structures.
While end-to-end approaches are currently favored, we believe
our method holds significant value for the following reasons:
(1) Our method has the potential to further improve the
topological performance of existing end-to-end methods. (2)
In situations where privacy concerns or limited data acces-
sibility prevent access to the original data, our method can
produce enhanced outcomes via analyzing shape information
alone. (3) Unlike end-to-end approaches, our method generates
new topologically critical regions without altering the original
output. This makes it more explainable and suitable for
interactive diagnosis. (4) Even when both image and label data
are inaccessible, our method can transfer the learned inherent
shape prior from other datasets to the target field.
In this paper, we introduce a novel framework that
redefines traditional morphological closing operations through
the integration of advanced deep learning techniques.
Our approach utilizes the reconstruction capabilities of a
trained masked AutoEncoder, which we term Deep Dilation,
to effectively highlight areas of disconnection. Additionally,
we have developed a module called Simple Point Erosion,
aimed at identifying topologically critical points by selectively
eroding non-essential ones (simple points). This further leads
to the design of a novel operation, Simple Component Erosion,
designed to eliminate topologically insignificant components
within structures.
Our proposed framework comprises these two innovative
operations. It demonstrates significant potential in identifying
regions of disconnection, thereby enhancing the topological
performance of medical tubular segmentation. Moreover,
our method exhibits a strong capability to transfer shape
priors from external datasets, showcasing its versatility and
effectiveness across different applications.
